verses.review_analysis: The declaration uses cursed from the earth, then personifies the earth as opening its mouth to receive the blood from Cain's hand. Keep both from phrases, the brother relationship and the hand image. The preposition after cursed can invite discussion of exclusion from the soil or the ground's involvement; do not resolve that question by replacing it with a different comparative construction.

verses.text: When you till the earth, it shall no longer yield its strength to you. You shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth.”
verses.display_text: When you till the earth, it shall no longer yield its strength to you. You shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth.”

verses.review_analysis: The tilling clause is introduced by an explanatory connective and leads to the ground no longer giving its strength. The inherited when gives the recurring circumstance naturally; for/because is the closer connective and remains an alternative for syntax review. The concluding state is groaning and trembling upon the earth, not an imported fugitive/wanderer pair. The close draft exposes the connective rather than silently claiming the two constructions identical.

verses.display_text: And Cain said to the Lord, “My guilt is too great for me to be forgiven.

verses.review_analysis: The comparison is my guilt/charge greater than my being forgiven. Guilt is a provisional sense of the accusation/responsibility noun; the infinitive is passive and its person is Cain. Retain too great for me to be forgiven instead of automatically importing punishment too great to bear. Whether the line is a despairing assertion or would benefit from interrogative English remains open; the printed running text uses a declarative presentation.

verses.text: If Thou dost cast me out this day from the face of the earth, I shall be hidden from Thy face; and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth, and whoever finds me shall slay me.”

verses.review_analysis: The response opens not so and contains a difficult sevenfold-vengeance construction, followed by the Lord God's placing a sign for Cain to prevent his killing by a finder. The inherited incur sevenfold vengeance is retained provisionally as the contextual consequence for the killer, not certified as a transparent word-for-word rendering of the unusual Greek verb/object combination. Mark does not identify a body location, physical form, ethnicity or hereditary trait. The difficult vengeance clause requires specialist and apparatus review.

verses.review_analysis: The selected verb is raised/high, with 150 days as duration. Remained high is a natural contextual rendering that avoids implying a new discrete upward movement each day. The duration is kept separate from the forty days of rain; their relationship requires narrative chronology, not arithmetic addition by default.

verses.review_analysis: The source explicitly gives the testing purpose and the raven's non-return until drying. That is retained rather than substituting going to and fro from another tradition. Until marks the stated limit but does not by itself prove that the raven returned afterward.

verses.review_analysis: The dove follows the raven. The masculine pronoun can refer back to the raven, making after it contextually apt; it is not changed to a claim that the dove flew physically behind Noah. The purpose and earth's face are retained without adding a new waiting interval.

verses.display_text: But the dove found no resting place for its feet, and returned to him in the ark, for water covered the whole face of the earth. And he stretched forth his hand, took it, and brought it to himself within the ark.

verses.review_analysis: Failure to find foot-rest motivates the return. Noah's three actions—reaching, taking and bringing inside—remain distinct, and the destination is repeated. verses.review_analysis: The source has an olive leaf followed by the difficult stalk/twig term. Inherited olive sprig with a leaf is a plausible construal, retained provisionally rather than certified as exact botany. Mouth is naturally beak for a bird. Freshly plucked is not inserted because this displayed word does not transparently say that.

inherited_unit.text: And he waited another seven days, and again sent forth the dove; and it returned to him no more.

verses.review_analysis: A second seven-day wait and another sending are explicit. The negative add-to-return idiom means it no longer returned. The inherited no more conveys this without retaining an awkward literal addition verb or inventing where the dove settled.

verses.text: And in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters had disappeared from the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark which he had made, and saw that the waters had disappeared from the face of the earth.
verses.display_text: And in the six hundred and first year of Noah’s life, in the first month, on the first day of the month, the waters had disappeared from the earth. And Noah removed the covering of the ark which he had made, and saw that the waters had disappeared from the face of the earth.

verses.review_analysis: The year is 601, with first month and first day. Removal/uncovering of the roof is distinct from the earlier window opening. The source repeats water's disappearance before and after Noah's observation, and the inherited English preserves that. Covering is retained as a broad roof term; it is not equated with the door.

verses.text: And the Lord God smelled the sweet fragrance, and the Lord God considered and said, “I will never again curse the earth because of the deeds of mankind, for the mind of man is bent intently upon evil from his youth. verses.review_analysis: The source repeats require three times, including beasts and a fellow human as accountable parties. The inherited English retains that sequence and the blood/life linkage. Surely expresses rhetorical weight rather than a separate certainty adverb. The precise brother/fellow-human construction deserves syntactic review; no class of exempt humans is added.

verses.review_analysis: The first divine title is Lord God and the repeated saying has Lord alone. The reporting verb is future plural they will say, whereas inherited it is said changes tense and voice. A customary or gnomic future can justify the inherited present as a contextual rendering; the future active is therefore a proposal exposing the Greek form, not proof that the inherited tense was wrong. Before remains neutral between presence and a more adversarial interpretation.

verses.text: And he himself went before them, and bowed down to the earth seven times, until he drew near to his brother.
verses.display_text: And he himself went before them, and bowed down to the earth seven times, until he drew near to his brother.

inherited_unit.text: And he himself went before them, and bowed down to the earth seven times, until he drew near to his brother.

verses.review_analysis: Jacob leads, with seven ground bows and progressive approach. The prostration verb here is social obeisance in context, not proof of worshiping Esau as divine. The count must not be reduced to a general repeated bow.

drafts.close: He himself went ahead and bowed to the ground seven times until near his brother.
drafts.spoken: And he himself went before them, and bowed down to the earth seven times, until he drew near to his brother.
drafts.literary: And he himself went before them, and bowed down to the earth seven times, until he drew near to his brother.

verses.text: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced and kissed him, and fell upon his neck; and they both wept.
verses.display_text: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced and kissed him, and fell upon his neck; and they both wept.

inherited_unit.text: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced and kissed him, and fell upon his neck; and they both wept.

verses.review_analysis: Both brothers weep, but Esau is the subject of the initial embrace. The source sequence and bodily image are preserved. No claim about the lasting resolution of all family conflict is added.

drafts.close: Esau ran to meet him, embraced and kissed him, fell on his neck, and both wept.
drafts.spoken: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced and kissed him, and fell upon his neck; and they both wept.
drafts.literary: And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced and kissed him, and fell upon his neck; and they both wept.

verses.text: And he lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, “Who are these with you?” And he said, “The children with whom God has shown mercy to your servant.”
verses.display_text: And he lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, “Who are these with you?” And he said, “The children with whom God has shown mercy to your servant.”

inherited_unit.text: And he lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, “Who are these with you?” And he said, “The children with whom God has shown mercy to your servant.”

verses.review_analysis: The relative mercy construction is rendered as children with whom God showed mercy, preserving God as giver in context. The question includes women and children though the answer focuses on children. Ordinary your servant addresses Esau, not God.

drafts.close: He saw the women and children and asked who they were; Jacob answered that God mercifully gave these children to his servant.
drafts.spoken: And he lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, “Who are these with you?” And he said, “The children with whom God has shown mercy to your servant.”
drafts.literary: And he lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children, and said, “Who are these with you?” And he said, “The children with whom God has shown mercy to your servant.”

verses.text: And the slave women and their children drew near, and bowed down.
verses.display_text: And the slave women and their children drew near, and bowed down.

inherited_unit.text: And the slave women and their children drew near, and bowed down.

verses.review_analysis: Both women and children share the approach and bowing. The source has children here rather than the earlier sons, and the inherited wording preserves it. This is the first of the three groups' responses.

drafts.close: The slave women and their children approached and bowed,
drafts.spoken: And the slave women and their children drew near, and bowed down.
drafts.literary: And the slave women and their children drew near, and bowed down.

verses.text: And Leah and her children drew near, and bowed down; and afterward Rachel and Joseph drew near, and bowed down.
verses.display_text: And Leah and her children drew near, and bowed down; and afterward Rachel and Joseph drew near, and bowed down.

inherited_unit.text: And Leah and her children drew near, and bowed down; and afterward Rachel and Joseph drew near, and bowed down.

verses.review_analysis: The order matches the arrangement in 33:2. Both approach and prostration repeat for the later group. Joseph's individual name remains rather than a generalized children label.

drafts.close: Leah and her children approached and bowed; afterward Rachel and Joseph did the same.
drafts.spoken: And Leah and her children drew near, and bowed down; and afterward Rachel and Joseph drew near, and bowed down.
drafts.literary: And Leah and her children drew near, and bowed down; and afterward Rachel and Joseph drew near, and bowed down.

verses.text: And he said, “What do you mean by all these companies which I met?” And he said, “That your servant may find grace in your sight, my lord.”
verses.display_text: And he said, “What do you mean by all these companies which I met?” And he said, “That your servant may find grace in your sight, my lord.”

inherited_unit.text: And he said, “What do you mean by all these companies which I met?” And he said, “That your servant may find grace in your sight, my lord.”

verses.review_analysis: Companies represents camps/groups, linking with the staged gifts. The purpose is gaining Esau's favor. My lord is a conventional English respectful address to a human and does not justify Thou forms.

drafts.close: He asked about all the companies he encountered; Jacob answered, so your servant may find favor before you, lord.
drafts.spoken: And he said, “What do you mean by all these companies which I met?” And he said, “That your servant may find grace in your sight, my lord.”
drafts.literary: And he said, “What do you mean by all these companies which I met?” And he said, “That your servant may find grace in your sight, my lord.”

verses.text: And Esau said, “I have much, brother; let what is yours be yours.”
verses.display_text: And Esau said, “I have much, brother; let what is yours be yours.”

inherited_unit.text: And Esau said, “I have much, brother; let what is yours be yours.”

verses.review_analysis: The affectionate brother address and refusal both remain. Much does not say Esau has literally everything, unlike Jacob's later expression. Let what is yours be yours keeps the source's possession repetition.

drafts.close: Esau said: I have much, brother; keep your own things.
drafts.spoken: And Esau said, “I have much, brother; let what is yours be yours.”
drafts.literary: And Esau said, “I have much, brother; let what is yours be yours.”

verses.text: And Jacob said, “If I have found grace in your sight, receive the gifts from my hands; for I have seen your face as one might see the face of God, and you will accept me.
verses.display_text: And Jacob said, “If I have found grace in your sight, receive the gifts from my hands; for I have seen your face as one might see the face of God, and you will accept me.

inherited_unit.text: And Jacob said, “If I have found grace in your sight, receive the gifts from my hands; for I have seen your face as one might see the face of God, and you will accept me.

verses.review_analysis: The source's final acceptance verb is future; it is not normalized to past you have accepted. The face comparison is preserved as a simile rather than identifying Esau with God. The gift request remains conditional on favor.

drafts.close: Jacob said: If I found favor, receive my gifts; I saw your face as one might see God's face, and you will accept me.
drafts.spoken: And Jacob said, “If I have found grace in your sight, receive the gifts from my hands; for I have seen your face as one might see the face of God, and you will accept me.
drafts.literary: And Jacob said, “If I have found grace in your sight, receive the gifts from my hands; for I have seen your face as one might see the face of God, and you will accept me.

verses.text: “Take my blessings which I have brought to you, for God has shown mercy to me, and I have all things.” And he urged him, and he took them.
verses.display_text: “Take my blessings which I have brought to you, for God has shown mercy to me, and I have all things.” And he urged him, and he took them.

inherited_unit.text: “Take my blessings which I have brought to you, for God has shown mercy to me, and I have all things.” And he urged him, and he took them.

verses.review_analysis: Blessings is plural and functions as the gifts in context. Jacob's urging precedes Esau's acceptance. Everything is the speaker's abundance claim, not an inventory declaration of universal ownership.

drafts.close: Take the blessings I brought, because God showed me mercy and I have everything; he pressed him, and he took them.
drafts.spoken: “Take my blessings which I have brought to you, for God has shown mercy to me, and I have all things.” And he urged him, and he took them.
drafts.literary: “Take my blessings which I have brought to you, for God has shown mercy to me, and I have all things.” And he urged him, and he took them.

verses.text: And he said, “Let us set out and go straight ahead.”
verses.display_text: And he said, “Let us set out and go straight ahead.”

inherited_unit.text: And he said, “Let us set out and go straight ahead.”

verses.review_analysis: The departure participle and future travel statement are naturally exhortative in context. The inherited let-us wording is retained. The selected Greek does not separately promise that Esau will lead Jacob as an escort.

drafts.close: He said: Let us set out, and we will go straight ahead.
drafts.spoken: And he said, “Let us set out and go straight ahead.”
drafts.literary: And he said, “Let us set out and go straight ahead.”

verses.text: And he said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and the sheep and cows under my care are nursing; if therefore I drive them hard for one day, all the livestock will die.
verses.display_text: And he said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and the sheep and cows under my care are nursing; if therefore I drive them hard for one day, all the livestock will die.

inherited_unit.text: And he said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and the sheep and cows under my care are nursing; if therefore I drive them hard for one day, all the livestock will die.

verses.review_analysis: The condition refers to hard driving for one day. Tender children and nursing animals supply two reasons for slower travel. The source does not specify milk production amounts or a modern husbandry timetable.

drafts.close: My lord knows the children are tender and the sheep and cows are nursing under my charge; driving them a day would kill all livestock.
drafts.spoken: And he said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and the sheep and cows under my care are nursing; if therefore I drive them hard for one day, all the livestock will die.
drafts.literary: And he said to him, “My lord knows that the children are tender, and the sheep and cows under my care are nursing; if therefore I drive them hard for one day, all the livestock will die.

verses.text: “Let my lord go before his servant; and I will make my way slowly, according to the journey before me and the children’s pace, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
verses.display_text: “Let my lord go before his servant; and I will make my way slowly, according to the journey before me and the children’s pace, until I come to my lord in Seir.”

inherited_unit.text: “Let my lord go before his servant; and I will make my way slowly, according to the journey before me and the children’s pace, until I come to my lord in Seir.”

verses.review_analysis: The difficult strengthening/proceeding verb is interpreted as making one's way. Leisurely progress and the children's pace remain. The promise to reach Seir is preserved as Jacob's speech, not rewritten to his later destination.

drafts.close: Let my lord go ahead; I will proceed at the journey's leisurely pace and the children's feet until I reach my lord in Seir.
drafts.spoken: “Let my lord go before his servant; and I will make my way slowly, according to the journey before me and the children’s pace, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
drafts.literary: “Let my lord go before his servant; and I will make my way slowly, according to the journey before me and the children’s pace, until I come to my lord in Seir.”

unresolved_questions: Strengthening/proceeding construction and the leisure-of-journey phrase need fuller syntax review.

verses.text: And Esau said, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” And he said, “Why this? It is enough that I have found grace in your sight, my lord.”
verses.display_text: And Esau said, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” And he said, “Why this? It is enough that I have found grace in your sight, my lord.”

inherited_unit.text: And Esau said, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” And he said, “Why this? It is enough that I have found grace in your sight, my lord.”

verses.review_analysis: The offer is of some companions, not a specified military unit. Jacob's sufficiency statement repeats the favor theme. The exchange does not name a reason for declining beyond the words given.

drafts.close: Esau offered to leave some people; Jacob replied, Why? Favor before you is enough, lord.
drafts.spoken: And Esau said, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” And he said, “Why this? It is enough that I have found grace in your sight, my lord.”
drafts.literary: And Esau said, “Let me leave with you some of the people who are with me.” And he said, “Why this? It is enough that I have found grace in your sight, my lord.”

verses.text: And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
verses.display_text: And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.

inherited_unit.text: And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.

verses.review_analysis: That day and Seir are explicit. Esau is the sole subject here; the line does not say Jacob accompanied him. The following change of route remains a distinct narrative action.

drafts.close: Esau returned that day along his way to Seir.
drafts.spoken: And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.
drafts.literary: And Esau returned that day on his way to Seir.

verses.text: And Jacob journeyed to Booths, and made houses for himself there, and made booths for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Booths.
verses.display_text: And Jacob journeyed to Booths, and made houses for himself there, and made booths for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Booths.

inherited_unit.text: And Jacob journeyed to Booths, and made houses for himself there, and made booths for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Booths.

verses.review_analysis: The source distinguishes plural human houses and animal booths. The place-name is translated to preserve its link with the shelters, not replaced by an unexplained Succoth. All three instances remain represented.

drafts.close: Jacob departed for Booths, made houses for himself and booths for livestock, and named the place Booths.
drafts.spoken: And Jacob journeyed to Booths, and made houses for himself there, and made booths for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Booths.
drafts.literary: And Jacob journeyed to Booths, and made houses for himself there, and made booths for his livestock; therefore he called the name of that place Booths.

verses.text: And Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he camped before the city.
verses.display_text: And Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he camped before the city.

inherited_unit.text: And Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he camped before the city.

verses.review_analysis: The displayed Greek treats Salem as a name; inherited Salem is retained rather than converting it to safely. The geographic relation to Shechem remains provisional, not a claim that the sites have been identified archaeologically.

drafts.close: Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem in Canaan, from Syrian Mesopotamia, and camped facing the city.
drafts.spoken: And Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he camped before the city.
drafts.literary: And Jacob came to Salem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Mesopotamia of Syria; and he camped before the city.

verses.text: And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred lambs.
verses.display_text: And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred lambs.

inherited_unit.text: And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred lambs.

verses.review_analysis: The price is one hundred lambs in this Greek, not pieces of silver. The seller is Hamor in the singular, not his sons. No ancient currency equivalence is asserted to resolve the unusual price expression.

drafts.close: He acquired the field portion where his tent stood from Hamor, Shechem's father, for 100 lambs.
drafts.spoken: And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred lambs.
drafts.literary: And he bought the portion of the field where he had pitched his tent from Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred lambs.

verses.text: And he set up an altar there, and called upon the God of Israel.
verses.display_text: And he set up an altar there, and called upon the God of Israel.

inherited_unit.text: And he set up an altar there, and called upon the God of Israel.

verses.review_analysis: Called upon is the selected invocation verb rather than named the altar. The relation of the indeclinable Israel to God is contextually taken as possessive; the close stage does not invent a divine name formula absent from the clause. Further syntax review remains open.

drafts.close: He set up an altar there and invoked the God of Israel.
drafts.spoken: And he set up an altar there, and called upon the God of Israel.
drafts.literary: And he set up an altar there, and called upon the God of Israel.

unresolved_questions: Attachment of indeclinable Israel in the invocation phrase needs specialist review.

verses.text: And Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the people of the land.
verses.display_text: And Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the people of the land.

inherited_unit.text: And Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the people of the land.

verses.review_analysis: Her parentage and purpose of seeing/learning about the local daughters remain. The source does not blame her for the violence that follows or specify a forbidden journey. People of the land renders the local inhabitants naturally.

drafts.close: Dinah, Leah's daughter borne to Jacob, went out to observe the local people's daughters.
drafts.spoken: And Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the people of the land.
drafts.literary: And Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of the people of the land.

verses.text: And Shechem the Horite, son of Hamor and ruler of the land, saw her, and seized her, and lay with her, and violated her.
verses.display_text: And Shechem the Horite, son of Hamor and ruler of the land, saw her, and seized her, and lay with her, and violated her.

inherited_unit.text: And Shechem the Horite, son of Hamor and ruler of the land, saw her, and seized her, and lay with her, and violated her.

verses.review_analysis: Horite is the displayed designation and is not changed to Hivite. Seized and violated convey the coercive, dishonoring sequence in context. The text gives no consent statement; the later affection language must not erase this action.

drafts.close: Shechem, Hamor's son, the Horite and land ruler, saw her, took her, lay with her and humiliated her.
drafts.spoken: And Shechem the Horite, son of Hamor and ruler of the land, saw her, and seized her, and lay with her, and violated her.
drafts.literary: And Shechem the Horite, son of Hamor and ruler of the land, saw her, and seized her, and lay with her, and violated her.

verses.text: And he was attached to the soul of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the maiden, and spoke to the maiden according to her heart.
verses.display_text: And he was attached to the soul of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the maiden, and spoke to the maiden according to her heart.

inherited_unit.text: And he was attached to the soul of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the maiden, and spoke to the maiden according to her heart.

verses.review_analysis: The attachment, love and speech are Shechem's actions and do not state Dinah reciprocated. Heart is an idiomatic rendering of the thought/mind expression. Its exact persuasive or tender nuance remains a lexical question, not a change to consensual romance.

drafts.close: He attached himself to Dinah's soul, loved the maiden and spoke according to her mind.
drafts.spoken: And he was attached to the soul of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the maiden, and spoke to the maiden according to her heart.
drafts.literary: And he was attached to the soul of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, and loved the maiden, and spoke to the maiden according to her heart.

unresolved_questions: The mind/heart speech phrase's precise sense remains unresolved; it cannot establish Dinah's consent.

verses.text: And Shechem spoke to Hamor his father, saying, “Take this young woman for me to be my wife.”
verses.display_text: And Shechem spoke to Hamor his father, saying, “Take this young woman for me to be my wife.”

inherited_unit.text: And Shechem spoke to Hamor his father, saying, “Take this young woman for me to be my wife.”

verses.review_analysis: The command is addressed to the father and concerns marriage. Young woman is contextual for the girl/servant term here; no new status of enslavement is inferred. Her wishes are not supplied where the source does not report them.

drafts.close: Shechem told his father Hamor: Obtain this young woman for me as wife.
drafts.spoken: And Shechem spoke to Hamor his father, saying, “Take this young woman for me to be my wife.”
drafts.literary: And Shechem spoke to Hamor his father, saying, “Take this young woman for me to be my wife.”

verses.text: And Jacob heard that the son of Hamor had defiled Dinah his daughter; but his sons were with his livestock in the plain, and Jacob kept silence until they came.
verses.display_text: And Jacob heard that the son of Hamor had defiled Dinah his daughter; but his sons were with his livestock in the plain, and Jacob kept silence until they came.

inherited_unit.text: And Jacob heard that the son of Hamor had defiled Dinah his daughter; but his sons were with his livestock in the plain, and Jacob kept silence until they came.

verses.review_analysis: The temporal waiting is explicit and not equated with approval. Livestock and field locate the sons. Defiled describes the assault's dishonoring effect in the narrative; it is not a narrator judgment that Dinah herself did wrong.

drafts.close: Jacob heard Hamor's son defiled Dinah; his sons were with livestock in the field, and he kept silent until they came.
drafts.spoken: And Jacob heard that the son of Hamor had defiled Dinah his daughter; but his sons were with his livestock in the plain, and Jacob kept silence until they came.
drafts.literary: And Jacob heard that the son of Hamor had defiled Dinah his daughter; but his sons were with his livestock in the plain, and Jacob kept silence until they came.

verses.text: And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.
verses.display_text: And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.

inherited_unit.text: And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.

verses.review_analysis: The father's role and purpose of conversation are explicit. The source does not yet introduce a formal treaty. Its simple movement clause should not be expanded with motives from the subsequent negotiation.

drafts.close: Hamor, Shechem's father, went to Jacob to speak with him.
drafts.spoken: And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.
drafts.literary: And Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him.

verses.text: And Jacob’s sons came from the plain; and when they heard, the men were deeply distressed, and were exceedingly grieved, because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter; and such a thing must not be.
verses.display_text: And Jacob’s sons came from the plain; and when they heard, the men were deeply distressed, and were exceedingly grieved, because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter; and such a thing must not be.

inherited_unit.text: And Jacob’s sons came from the plain; and when they heard, the men were deeply distressed, and were exceedingly grieved, because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter; and such a thing must not be.

verses.review_analysis: The source emphasizes distress rather than a separately named anger verb. The concluding future can express what must not happen, represented by inherited must not be. The moral condemnation targets the act, not Dinah.

drafts.close: Jacob's sons came, heard and were deeply distressed because a disgrace was done in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter; such a thing shall not be.
drafts.spoken: And Jacob’s sons came from the plain; and when they heard, the men were deeply distressed, and were exceedingly grieved, because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter; and such a thing must not be.
drafts.literary: And Jacob’s sons came from the plain; and when they heard, the men were deeply distressed, and were exceedingly grieved, because he had done a disgraceful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob’s daughter; and such a thing must not be.

verses.text: And Hamor spoke to them, saying, “Shechem my son has set his soul upon your daughter; therefore give her to him to be his wife.
verses.display_text: And Hamor spoke to them, saying, “Shechem my son has set his soul upon your daughter; therefore give her to him to be his wife.

inherited_unit.text: And Hamor spoke to them, saying, “Shechem my son has set his soul upon your daughter; therefore give her to him to be his wife.

verses.review_analysis: Set his soul upon renders the volitional attachment. Your is plural addressing the family, not a claim that all are her biological fathers. The request is Hamor's, without a reported reply from Dinah.

drafts.close: Hamor said: My son chose your daughter with his soul; give her to him as wife.
drafts.spoken: And Hamor spoke to them, saying, “Shechem my son has set his soul upon your daughter; therefore give her to him to be his wife.
drafts.literary: And Hamor spoke to them, saying, “Shechem my son has set his soul upon your daughter; therefore give her to him to be his wife.

verses.text: “Intermarry with us; give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for your sons.
verses.display_text: “Intermarry with us; give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for your sons.

inherited_unit.text: “Intermarry with us; give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for your sons.

verses.review_analysis: The two-way marriage proposal and explicit for your sons clause are retained. The source addresses the group plurally. It does not say an agreement has already been reached.

drafts.close: Intermarry with us: give your daughters and take ours for your sons.
drafts.spoken: “Intermarry with us; give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for your sons.
drafts.literary: “Intermarry with us; give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for your sons.

verses.text: “And live among us; behold, the land is broad before you. Live and trade in it, and acquire possessions in it.”
verses.display_text: “And live among us; behold, the land is broad before you. Live and trade in it, and acquire possessions in it.”

inherited_unit.text: “And live among us; behold, the land is broad before you. Live and trade in it, and acquire possessions in it.”

verses.review_analysis: Three economic/residential invitations remain alongside the broad-land statement. Trade is the selected commercial verb, not a promise of free travel only. No additional land grant or citizenship status is asserted.

drafts.close: Live among us; the land is broad before you: settle, trade and acquire property in it.
drafts.spoken: “And live among us; behold, the land is broad before you. Live and trade in it, and acquire possessions in it.”
drafts.literary: “And live among us; behold, the land is broad before you. Live and trade in it, and acquire possessions in it.”

verses.text: And Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find grace in your sight, and whatever you say, we will give.
verses.display_text: And Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find grace in your sight, and whatever you say, we will give.

inherited_unit.text: And Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find grace in your sight, and whatever you say, we will give.

verses.review_analysis: The speaker begins with I and ends with plural we will give. The inherited text correctly preserves that shift, rather than normalizing every pronoun to singular. The recipients remain both father and brothers.

drafts.close: Shechem said to her father and brothers: May I find favor before you; whatever you ask, we will give.
drafts.spoken: And Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find grace in your sight, and whatever you say, we will give.
drafts.literary: And Shechem said to her father and to her brothers, “Let me find grace in your sight, and whatever you say, we will give.

verses.text: “Make the marriage payment exceedingly great, and I will give according to whatever you say to me; and give me this young woman to be my wife.”
verses.display_text: “Make the marriage payment exceedingly great, and I will give according to whatever you say to me; and give me this young woman to be my wife.”

inherited_unit.text: “Make the marriage payment exceedingly great, and I will give according to whatever you say to me; and give me this young woman to be my wife.”

verses.review_analysis: The source names a marriage payment and an emphatic amount, not a separately stated additional gift. The first-person future returns to singular. The final request is naturally imperative in English, with its source future form noted as a contextual function.

verses.review_analysis: The repeated Jacob and the new Israel are retained. This renewed naming statement is not deleted because of chapter 32. The text does not imply every subsequent use of Jacob is an error to normalize away.

verses.review_analysis: The departure and location of speech remain. He is devotional capitalization for the divine speaker, supported by the named subject. A destination such as heaven is not added where this clause omits it.

verses.review_analysis: The source explicitly names God in the relative clause. The repeated naming is preserved rather than treated as redundant. The inherited word order is natural without changing the place into the pillar as the object named.

verses.review_analysis: The explanatory dying clause is explicit. The mother's name is translated semantically, while Benjamin remains a name. Soul-departure imagery is preserved without claiming the verse resolves a philosophical account of death.

drafts.close: As she released her soul, for she was dying, she named him Son of My Sorrow; his father called him Benjamin.

verses.review_analysis: The pillar, tomb and narrator's to-this-day claim are all retained. It does not verify the survival of a particular modern monument. The next stored unit is 35:22; no missing verse is manufactured.

verses.review_analysis: The source includes Israel's adverse assessment and then the twelve-son summary within the same unit. The sexual act is stated without invented consent or additional circumstance. The switch of Israel/Jacob names is preserved.

verses.review_analysis: The explicit total is 180. The inherited hundred and eighty agrees. The verse gives a lifespan without a standalone absolute date; it is not combined with unrelated ages to force a historical chronology.

verses.review_analysis: The source's expiring verb is expanded as his strength failed in the inherited reading; that is a contextual expression, not an explicit strength noun. Family represents kindred. Both sons and their order as buriers remain.

verses.review_analysis: The source identifies Esau with Edom in a parenthetical clause. The inherited wording preserves that identification and the genealogical heading. It does not independently equate every later group named Edom with one individual.

verses.review_analysis: The three goods and Gilead-to-Egypt route remain. Spices is a broad inherited rendering of incense/aromatics; stacte is retained pending specialist commodity identification. The text does not specify the goods' modern botanical species or prices.

drafts.close: They sat to eat bread and saw Ishmaelite travelers from Gilead with camels laden with incense, resin and stacte, going down to Egypt.

unresolved_questions: Aromatics, resin and stacte require specialist commodity/lexical study.

verses.review_analysis: The women contrast Hebrew and Egyptian childbirth and say births occur before the midwives enter. The final and they bore is present in the source after the quoted explanation. Preserve that narration without adding a biological theory or independently judging the truthfulness of every part of their reply.

verses.review_analysis: The opened basket contains a weeping child, whom the princess spares or regards with compassion. Had compassion is a contextual rendering of the same general sparing verb discussed in the Jonah proposal; that does not require mechanically identical English. She identifies him as one of the Hebrew children.

verses.review_analysis: The sister offers to call a nursing woman from among the Hebrews, who will nurse the child for the princess. The speaker remains the sister, not the mother. The two for-you relationships are represented without making the princess the physical nurse.

verses.review_analysis: The princess gives a singular go command. The young woman then calls the child’s mother. Young woman is the source’s age-category term; no exact age is supplied, and the mother is not falsely described as an unrelated nurse.

verses.review_analysis: The princess commands keeping and nursing the child for her, then promises wages. The woman takes the child and nurses him. Repeated for me preserves the princess’s claimed relationship, while the narrative nursing agent remains the woman.

verses.review_analysis: Many days pass and Moses grows before going to his brothers, identified as Israel’s sons. He observes their suffering and an Egyptian striking one of those brothers. The repeated kinship labels remain, and the historical present is rendered as narrative past.

verses.review_analysis: Moses looks in both directions, sees no one, strikes the Egyptian and hides him in sand. Struck down is supported by the subsequent account of killing. verses.text: King Baltasar held a great reception on the day of the dedication of his royal buildings and invited two thousand men from among his magnates. On that day Baltasar, elated by wine and boasting, praised all the nations’ cast and carved gods in his place, but gave no praise to God Most High. That very night fingers like a human’s came out and inscribed on the plaster of his house’s wall, opposite the lamp, “Mane, Phares, Thekel.” Their interpretation is: Mane, “It has been numbered”; Phares, “It has been taken away”; Thekel, “It has been weighed.”

inherited_unit.text: They said to him, “Tell us on whose account this calamity is among us. What is your occupation? Where do you come from? What country and what people are you from?”
inherited_unit.display_text: They said to him, “Tell us on whose account this calamity is among us. What is your occupation? Where do you come from? What country and what people are you from?”

verses.review_analysis: The question about the calamity is retained even after the lot has identified Jonah. The four questions concern work, point of departure, country and people. Smoothing the last two into a coordinated question does not merge country with ethnic affiliation. No answer such as Hebrew is imported from another textual tradition.

verses.text: He said to them, “I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”
verses.display_text: He said to them, “I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

inherited_unit.text: He said to them, “I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”
inherited_unit.display_text: He said to them, “I am a servant of the Lord, and I worship the Lord, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

verses.review_analysis: The displayed Greek identifies Jonah as a servant of the Lord; that reading is retained rather than replaced by a familiar Hebrew-based self-identification. Worship renders the verb of reverence without converting it into a claim about his conduct. The Lord is identified as God of heaven and maker of the sea and dry land, both creation objects being preserved.

verses.text: The men were greatly afraid and said to him, “What is this you have done?” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.
verses.display_text: The men were greatly afraid and said to him, “What is this you have done?” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

inherited_unit.text: The men were greatly afraid and said to him, “What is this you have done?” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.
inherited_unit.display_text: The men were greatly afraid and said to him, “What is this you have done?” For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the Lord, because he had told them.

verses.review_analysis: Greatly afraid represents the cognate verb/noun expression of great fear. The sailors' question is followed by two causal explanations: they knew Jonah was fleeing because he had told them. The inherited pluperfect appropriately locates his disclosure before their reaction. The repeated subject men is retained in the explanatory clause.

verses.text: They said to him, “What shall we do to you, so that the sea may subside for us?” For the sea kept raising a greater surge.
verses.display_text: They said to him, “What shall we do to you, so that the sea may subside for us?” For the sea kept raising a greater surge.

inherited_unit.text: They said to him, “What shall we do to you, so that the sea may subside for us?” For the sea kept raising a greater surge.
inherited_unit.display_text: They said to him, “What shall we do to you, so that the sea may subside for us?” For the sea kept raising a greater surge.

verses.review_analysis: The question joins the action toward Jonah with the sea's prospective subsiding. English so that expresses the expected outcome of the Greek coordinated future construction without changing the addressees. The continued intensification of the sea is retained in kept raising a greater surge. This is not an instruction from the narrator to harm Jonah.

verses.text: Jonah said to them, “Lift me up and throw me into the sea; then the sea will subside for you. For I know that this great surge is upon you because of me.”
verses.display_text: Jonah said to them, “Lift me up and throw me into the sea; then the sea will subside for you. For I know that this great surge is upon you because of me.”

inherited_unit.text: Jonah said to them, “Lift me up and throw me into the sea; then the sea will subside for you. For I know that this great surge is upon you because of me.”
inherited_unit.display_text: Jonah said to them, “Lift me up and throw me into the sea; then the sea will subside for you. For I know that this great surge is upon you because of me.”

verses.review_analysis: Jonah directs the men to lift and throw him into the sea, with subsiding as the stated result. He identifies himself as the reason for this great surge. I know is appropriate for the resulting state conveyed by the Greek perfect; it is not weakened to speculation. You is plural here, though ordinary English does not mark that number.

verses.text: But the men strained to return to land and could not, for the sea kept rising more fiercely against them.
verses.display_text: But the men strained to return to land and could not, for the sea kept rising more fiercely against them.

inherited_unit.text: But the men strained to return to land and could not, for the sea kept rising more fiercely against them.
inherited_unit.display_text: But the men strained to return to land and could not, for the sea kept rising more fiercely against them.

verses.review_analysis: The men strive to return toward land but are unable. The purposive infinitive and explicit negative are retained. The text does not specify rowing, so strained remains suitably general. The continued, intensified movement of the sea against them explains their inability and parallels the preceding increase.

verses.text: They cried out to the Lord and said, “By no means, Lord! May we not perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for Thou, Lord, hast done as Thou didst wish.”
verses.display_text: They cried out to the Lord and said, “By no means, Lord! May we not perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for Thou, Lord, hast done as Thou didst wish.”

inherited_unit.text: They cried out to the Lord and said, “By no means, Lord! May we not perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for Thou, Lord, hast done as Thou didst wish.”
inherited_unit.display_text: They cried out to the Lord and said, “By no means, Lord! May we not perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood upon us, for Thou, Lord, hast done as Thou didst wish.”

verses.review_analysis: The sailors petition the Lord not to let them perish on account of this man's life and not to charge them with innocent blood. Innocent renders the blood adjective in this juridical plea, without certifying Jonah's entire character. The strongly negative opening and subsequent prohibition are both represented. Thou/hast/didst follow direct singular divine address; the conclusion concerns God's action according to His will.

verses.text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.
verses.display_text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

inherited_unit.text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.
inherited_unit.display_text: They took Jonah and threw him out into the sea, and the sea stopped its tossing.

verses.review_analysis: The men take Jonah and throw him out into the sea; the sea then ceases its tossing. The distinct action and result are retained. The sentence does not yet include the sea creature, which belongs to the following source-numbered chapter. No miraculous mechanism beyond the stated cessation is added.

verses.text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.
verses.display_text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

inherited_unit.text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.
inherited_unit.display_text: The men feared the Lord with great fear, offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows.

verses.review_analysis: Fear with great fear, sacrifice to the Lord and vows form the sailors' response. The inherited wording retains the emphatic fear expression, the Lord as object/recipient and the sequence of sacrifice and vows. It does not explain the practical timing of sacrifice or import a later conversion narrative.

verses.text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.
verses.display_text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

inherited_unit.text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.
inherited_unit.display_text: The Lord commanded a great sea creature to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the sea creature’s belly three days and three nights.

verses.review_analysis: The Lord commands a great sea creature to swallow Jonah. The creature's size is explicit, but a modern species is not. Three days and three nights and Jonah's location in the belly are retained. This is source-numbered 2:1, not silently reassigned to 1:17; the chapter division is part of the edition's stable identity.

verses.text: Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,
verses.display_text: Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,

inherited_unit.text: Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,
inherited_unit.display_text: Jonah prayed to the Lord his God from the sea creature’s belly,

verses.review_analysis: Jonah prays to the Lord his God from the creature's belly. The possessive and location are retained, and the comma continues into the next unit's introduction of speech. Prayer is not described as occurring after emergence. The verse boundary and open syntactic continuation remain intact.

verses.text: and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.
verses.display_text: and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.

inherited_unit.text: and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.
inherited_unit.display_text: and said: “In my affliction I cried to the Lord my God, and He listened to me. From the belly of Hades Thou didst hear the voice of my cry.

verses.review_analysis: The first clause narrates Jonah's cry in distress and God's listening; the second turns to direct divine address. Hades remains a named underworld image rather than a doctrinal expansion. Voice of my cry is an English synthesis of the displayed cry/voice genitives; the precise attachment remains a syntax-review item, not a claim of exhaustive alignment. The change from He to Thou follows the source's person change.
unresolved_questions: Attachment of cry and voice genitives.

verses.text: Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.
verses.display_text: Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.

inherited_unit.text: Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.
inherited_unit.display_text: Thou didst cast me into the depths of the heart of the sea, and rivers encircled me. All Thy billows and Thy waves passed over me.

verses.review_analysis: God is addressed as the one who cast Jonah into sea-depths. Rivers and the two wave terms remain separate images; the repeated divine possessive is retained. All qualifies the billows in the coordinated phrase. The candidate neither relocates the setting to a literal river nor removes the poem's images in favor of an explanatory paraphrase.

verses.text: I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’
verses.display_text: I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’

inherited_unit.text: I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’
inherited_unit.display_text: I said, ‘I have been thrust away from Thine eyes. Shall I again look toward Thy holy sanctuary?’

verses.review_analysis: The speaker's banishment from God's eyes and the question about looking again toward the sanctuary are retained. The question particle is not replaced by an unconditional assurance that he will return. Again is warranted by the construction meaning to add/continue to look, unlike an ornamental insertion. Sanctuary is the inherited rendering of the temple noun; its exact contextual referent remains for review.
unresolved_questions: Force of the question and sanctuary referent.

verses.text: Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.
verses.display_text: Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.

inherited_unit.text: Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.
inherited_unit.display_text: Water poured around me up to my life; the uttermost abyss encircled me; my head sank into clefts of mountains.

verses.review_analysis: The verse has enclosing water, the uttermost abyss and the head's descent into mountain clefts. The difficult expression reaching as far as life is retained provisionally rather than changed to neck from another language or tradition. Up to my life is awkward English and needs a better Greek-grounded spoken draft. The imagery is not converted into a geographical or anatomical claim.
unresolved_questions: An idiomatic rendering of the life-threatening water expression that accounts for the selected Greek.

verses.text: I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints; and let the ruin of my life rise up, Lord my God.
verses.display_text: I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints; and let the ruin of my life rise up, Lord my God.

inherited_unit.text: I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints; and let the ruin of my life rise up, Lord my God.
inherited_unit.display_text: I descended into a land whose bars are everlasting restraints; and let the ruin of my life rise up, Lord my God.

verses.review_analysis: The land's bars/restraints are everlasting, followed by a third-person imperative with ruin/corruption as its apparent nominative subject. The inherited let the ruin of my life rise up preserves that difficult surface construction. It is NOT treated as a resolved translation: the sense and genitive attachment require specialist syntax, broader usage and apparatus comparison. The wording must not be silently changed to an accomplished Thou didst bring up my life, which is not this displayed Greek construction.
unresolved_questions: Sense of ruin/corruption as apparent subject of the imperative; genitive attachment; relevant apparatus and broader Greek usage.

verses.text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.
verses.display_text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.

inherited_unit.text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.
inherited_unit.display_text: As my life was failing me, I remembered the Lord; may my prayer come to Thee, into Thy holy sanctuary.

verses.review_analysis: The temporal infinitival construction places recollection of the Lord during the failing of Jonah's life. The following optative is retained as a wish, may my prayer come, not as a report that the prayer already arrived. Direct Thee/Thy follows the shift back to address. Into the holy sanctuary preserves the source's destination image.

verses.text: Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.
verses.display_text: Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.

inherited_unit.text: Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.
inherited_unit.display_text: Those who guard vain and false things abandoned their mercy.

verses.review_analysis: The subject is people attending to vain and false things; abandoned retains the aorist predicate instead of automatically converting it to a present maxim. Their mercy preserves the possessive but leaves its referent unresolved: mercy they should show or mercy available to them need contextual/lexical review. Guard is formally close yet may obscure attending to or observing; no accepted replacement is claimed.
unresolved_questions: Sense of observing/guarding and referent of their mercy.

verses.text: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”
verses.display_text: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

inherited_unit.text: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”
inherited_unit.display_text: But I, with a voice of praise and thanksgiving, will sacrifice to Thee. Whatever I vowed I will repay to Thee, for deliverance to the Lord!”

verses.review_analysis: The contrastive I, voiced praise and thanksgiving, future sacrifice and repayment of vows are retained. The final genitive form relating to deliverance followed by to the Lord is syntactically difficult; the inherited for deliverance to the Lord is provisional and not idiomatic resolved English. It must not be recast as the familiar Salvation belongs to the Lord without evidence that this accounts for the selected Greek syntax. Lexical sense and attachment remain explicit open issues.
unresolved_questions: Function and attachment of the final genitive deliverance expression and dative to the Lord; idiomatic English remains unresolved.

verses.text: The sea creature was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto dry land.
verses.display_text: The sea creature was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto dry land.

inherited_unit.text: The sea creature was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto dry land.
inherited_unit.display_text: The sea creature was commanded, and it cast Jonah out onto dry land.

verses.review_analysis: The displayed passive states that the sea creature was commanded, without an expressed agent in this clause. The inherited passive therefore avoids adding the Lord as an explicit grammatical subject. It then expels Jonah onto dry land. The repeated creature designation and the destination are retained without implying a species.

verses.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:
verses.display_text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:

inherited_unit.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:
inherited_unit.display_text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time, saying:

verses.review_analysis: The word comes to Jonah a second time, explicitly linking this commission with the first. Second time is a stated feature, not inferred repetition. The inherited introductory sentence and colon retain the recipient, divine source and speech transition; the initial narrative conjunction is represented by the sequence of sentences rather than a separate And.

verses.text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you.”
verses.display_text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you.”

inherited_unit.text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you.”
inherited_unit.display_text: “Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it according to the former proclamation that I spoke to you.”

verses.review_analysis: Rising, going and proclaiming are again commanded to Jonah singular. The proclamation is tied to the former message already spoken to him. The inherited English preserves that backward reference instead of changing it to an unspecified future message. Nineveh's great-city description and proclamation within it are both retained.

verses.text: Jonah rose and went to Nineveh as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a city great before God, about a three-day journey.
verses.display_text: Jonah rose and went to Nineveh as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a city great before God, about a three-day journey.

inherited_unit.text: Jonah rose and went to Nineveh as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a city great before God, about a three-day journey.
inherited_unit.display_text: Jonah rose and went to Nineveh as the Lord had spoken. Now Nineveh was a city great before God, about a three-day journey.

verses.review_analysis: Jonah rises and goes in accordance with the Lord's speech. Great before God keeps the explicit divine dative visible, although an intensive interpretation of the phrase remains possible. The approximate three-day journey is not turned into a precise diameter, circumference or modern distance; the Greek itself does not supply that geographical clarification.
unresolved_questions: Divine dative's force and exact journey measure.

verses.text: And Jonah began to enter the city, about a day’s journey, and he proclaimed and said, “Three more days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
verses.display_text: And Jonah began to enter the city, about a day’s journey, and he proclaimed and said, “Three more days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

inherited_unit.text: And Jonah began to enter the city, about a day’s journey, and he proclaimed and said, “Three more days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
inherited_unit.display_text: And Jonah began to enter the city, about a day’s journey, and he proclaimed and said, “Three more days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”

verses.review_analysis: The approximate one-day entry, the two speech verbs and the three-day warning are retained. The displayed Rahlfs–Hanhart running text reads three, so forty is not substituted from familiar versions. The future passive leaves the overthrowing agent implicit. These are source-specific observations, not a new manuscript/apparatus collation.

verses.text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.
verses.display_text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.

inherited_unit.text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.
inherited_unit.display_text: The people of Nineveh believed God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth, from their greatest to their least.

verses.review_analysis: The Ninevites believe God, proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth from greatest to least. People is a contextual collective rendering of the word for men here; it does not assert a different census. Greatest/least preserves social breadth without forcing an age-only interpretation. The plural action remains separate from the king's response in the next unit.

verses.text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.
verses.display_text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.

inherited_unit.text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.
inherited_unit.display_text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.

verses.review_analysis: The report reaches the king, who rises, removes his robe, puts on sackcloth and sits in ashes. The sequence and royal contrast are retained. Off himself represents the reflexive wording. No explanation of court ritual or extra confession is inserted into the Scripture sentence.

verses.text: It was proclaimed and declared in Nineveh from the king and his nobles: “Let people and livestock, cattle and sheep, taste nothing; let them not graze or drink water.”
verses.display_text: It was proclaimed and declared in Nineveh from the king and his nobles: “Let people and livestock, cattle and sheep, taste nothing; let them not graze or drink water.”

inherited_unit.text: It was proclaimed and declared in Nineveh from the king and his nobles: “Let people and livestock, cattle and sheep, taste nothing; let them not graze or drink water.”
inherited_unit.display_text: It was proclaimed and declared in Nineveh from the king and his nobles: “Let people and livestock, cattle and sheep, taste nothing; let them not graze or drink water.”

verses.review_analysis: The passive proclamation comes from the king and his nobles. The prohibition separately names people, livestock, cattle and sheep, and forbids tasting, grazing and drinking water. The repeated negatives are represented by taste nothing and let them not. The inherited quotation ends here because the following Greek verbs narrate actions rather than continuing imperative commands.

verses.text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:
verses.display_text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:

inherited_unit.text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:
inherited_unit.display_text: People and livestock clothed themselves in sackcloth, and they cried earnestly to God. Each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice in their hands, saying:

verses.review_analysis: The Greek now narrates sackcloth, earnest crying and turning with past indicative verbs. The candidate preserves that form instead of harmonizing them into commands. Each with his evil way and their hands retains the source's shift between distributive singular and collective plural. The shared subject including livestock is not silently rewritten, though the practical distribution of actions is an interpretation issue.
unresolved_questions: Distribution of narrated actions over people and animals; distributive singular/plural shift.

verses.text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we shall not perish?”
verses.display_text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we shall not perish?”

inherited_unit.text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we certainly do not perish?”
inherited_unit.display_text: “Who knows whether God will relent and turn from His fierce anger, so that we certainly do not perish?”

verses.review_analysis: Propose a natural future result clause: so that we shall not perish. The displayed emphatic negative with a subjunctive expresses non-perishing, but certainly do not is awkward under the opening who-knows question and can sound like an independent present guarantee. The question remains conditional on God's possible relenting; shall not carries the firm negative without adding an assurance outside that question. His fierce anger represents the paired wrath terms. Full mood/discourse review remains open.
unresolved_questions: Independent review of mood, emphatic negation and the result clause within the who-knows question.

verses.text: God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.
verses.display_text: God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.

inherited_unit.text: God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.
inherited_unit.display_text: God saw their deeds, that they had turned from their evil ways. God relented concerning the calamity He had said He would bring upon them, and He did not do it.

verses.review_analysis: God sees their deeds, specifically their turning from evil ways, and relents concerning the threatened calamity. The inherited wording preserves the object of relenting and the explicit final non-performance. It neither changes deeds into words alone nor adds a theological account of divine repentance. The repeated God and the final He did not do it remain visible.

verses.text: Jonah was grieved with great grief and was disturbed.
verses.display_text: Jonah was grieved with great grief and was disturbed.

inherited_unit.text: Jonah was grieved with great grief and was disturbed.
inherited_unit.display_text: Jonah was grieved with great grief and was disturbed.

verses.review_analysis: The selected Greek emphasizes grief with a cognate noun and adds disturbance/confusion. Grieved with great grief and disturbed retain both rather than importing anger as the sole description from familiar renderings. No psychological diagnosis is inferred. The verse's contrast with the city's rescue is left to the narrative context.

verses.text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.
verses.display_text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

inherited_unit.text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.
inherited_unit.display_text: He prayed to the Lord and said, “O Lord, were these not my words while I was still in my own land? That is why I was quick to flee to Tarshish, for I knew that Thou art merciful and compassionate, patient, abundant in mercy, and relenting concerning calamities.

verses.review_analysis: Jonah's prayer recalls his earlier words at home and links his prior flight with his knowledge of God's character. The source lists mercy, compassion, patience, abundant mercy and relenting over calamities; all are retained. Thou art follows singular divine address. Was quick to flee is a provisional contextual rendering of the anticipatory verb; its exact temporal nuance remains open rather than an etymology-based certainty.
unresolved_questions: Precise nuance of the anticipatory flight verb.

verses.text: And now, Master Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
verses.display_text: And now, Master Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”

inherited_unit.text: And now, Master Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”
inherited_unit.display_text: And now, Master Lord, take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live.”

verses.review_analysis: The compound divine address Master Lord is retained. The imperative asks God to take Jonah's life; the reason compares dying with living. The inherited better than construction naturally renders the comparison without adding now to the death wish beyond the opening and now. No moral judgment about Jonah's request is supplied in the verse.

verses.text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”
verses.display_text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”

inherited_unit.text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”
inherited_unit.display_text: The Lord said to Jonah, “Are you deeply grieved?”

verses.review_analysis: The Lord asks whether Jonah is greatly grieved. The intensifying adverb is rendered deeply, and ordinary you is used because Jonah, not God, is addressed. The Greek question here is not silently changed into the familiar question whether Jonah is right to be angry. The state expressed by the perfect is retained in the English present description.

verses.review_analysis: The Lord God commands the gourd; its growth over Jonah's head supplies shade and protection from his troubles. The source's repeated head/shading language is substantially retained, along with great joy in parallel to the earlier great grief. Gourd is the inherited general botanical designation, not a confirmed modern species. The troubles may include discomfort and distress; no single diagnosis is imposed.
unresolved_questions: Botanical identification; scope of troubles.

verses.review_analysis: The next-day dawn, God's command to a worm, the worm's striking of the gourd and its drying are retained. verses.review_analysis: The sunrise triggers a commanded hot, scorching wind, then the sun strikes Jonah's head. The two heat expressions and striking repetition are retained. Lost heart follows the Greek verb rather than asserting a medical faint; renounced his life is a provisional rendering of the refusal/disavowal expression. Jonah repeats the preference for death, without an added account of attempted self-harm.
unresolved_questions: Contextual nuance of losing heart and renouncing life.

verses.review_analysis: God repeats the question about great grief, now explicitly concerning the gourd. Jonah replies with the same intensity and the limit even to death. Ordinary singular you preserves the addressee policy, while I retains the response's emphasis. The candidate does not turn the question into a moral right-to-anger formula absent from this displayed wording.

verses.text: The Lord said, “You had pity on the gourd, over which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came to be in a night and perished in a night.
verses.display_text: The Lord said, “You had pity on the gourd, over which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came to be in a night and perished in a night.

inherited_unit.text: The Lord said, “You spared the gourd, over which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came to be in a night and perished in a night.
inherited_unit.display_text: The Lord said, “You spared the gourd, over which you did not toil and which you did not nurture, which came to be in a night and perished in a night.

verses.review_analysis: Propose had pity on for the past form of pheidomai with the gourd as its concern. In context Jonah mourned its loss; You spared can misleadingly imply that he successfully preserved it. The same verb recurs in 4:11, where the proposed have pity on preserves that link. Middle Liddell was consulted for the general range of sparing, mercy and care; the choice here is a contextual inference, not a specialist LXX entry or apparatus verdict. The denied labor/nurture and repeated night are unchanged.
unresolved_questions: Specialist LXX review of pheidomai with hyper; whether pity or spare best preserves the two-verse analogy.

verses.text: And shall I not have pity on Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

inherited_unit.text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”
inherited_unit.display_text: And shall I not spare Nineveh, the great city, in which dwell more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know their right from their left, and much livestock?”

verses.review_analysis: Propose have pity on to match the same verb in 4:10 while retaining the divine first-person future question. Its contextual implication includes sparing the city, not merely an abstract emotion. The great-city description, more than 120,000 people, right/left ignorance and many livestock are retained. The people are not identified as infants, and the concluding question is not replaced by a doctrinal explanation. The lexical choice remains a proposal requiring review.
unresolved_questions: Same lexical decision as 4:10; retain sparing as a contextual implication of pity.
